narrative: The model estimated a 60.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, which is why your law school application was denied. This does not mean failure is certain; it means that, on the information available, the risk was judged too high for admission at this stage. The decision was driven mainly by your academic standing in law school rather than by your LSAT alone. Your LSAT score of 46 was the single most influential factor and it worked in your favor—well above the accepted-student average of about 37—pushing the prediction toward passing. However, your Year 3 decile was the second most influential factor and pushed strongly toward failure; at 3, it is well below the accepted-student average near 5.8. Your Year 1 decile was the third most influential factor and also pushed toward failure; at 3, it is below the accepted average of about 6. Together, these two academic-standing indicators outweighed the positive LSAT signal and produced the overall fail prediction. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.5 was above the accepted average and was not among the top drivers. Next, ask admissions for feedback, focus on raising your standing in upper-year coursework or explaining any grade trend, and consult an academic advisor about a plan to demonstrate bar-exam readiness. You may also consider delaying reapplication until you have stronger academic evidence or additional preparation, and ask whether a holistic review or conditional pathway is available.
